items.prompt: Why is a body normally very unlikely to become a fossil at all?

options.label: Because scavengers and decay usually destroy a body before it can be buried
options.feedback: Scavengers, bacteria, and weather typically finish off soft tissue and scatter bone within a short time, well before sediment has a chance to cover it.

options.label: Because most environments are too cold for fossils to form
options.feedback: Cold slows decay rather than blocking fossilization outright; fossils form in warm places too, wherever burial happens quickly enough.

options.label: Because bones are too heavy to be carried by water
options.feedback: Bones are frequently moved and scattered by water; that scattering is part of what usually keeps them from being preserved together.

options.label: Because most animals have no bones to preserve
options.feedback: Most animals that leave a rich fossil record, from dinosaurs to mammoths, had a bony skeleton to begin with.

items.ok_line: A race against decay, and burial almost always loses.
items.ko_line: Think about what normally happens to a body in the days after death, before anything can bury it.
items.exp_title: A race that burial usually loses
items.exp_text: The moment an animal dies, scavengers, insects, and bacteria set to work on the soft tissue, and wind, water, and trampling scatter whatever bone is left behind. For a fossil to form, sediment such as mud, sand, or ash has to cover the remains before that destruction finishes its work. Most bodies lose that race entirely, which is why a fossil represents an accident of fast burial rather than the ordinary fate of a body.

items.prompt: How does a bone buried in sediment gradually turn into solid rock, a process called permineralization?

options.label: Heat and pressure melt the bone into a new mineral
options.feedback: Melting would destroy the bone's structure; permineralization instead leaves the original shape intact, right down to fine internal detail.

options.label: The bone dries out completely and turns to dust
options.feedback: A dried, crumbled bone would leave nothing to fossilize; permineralization instead adds mineral material rather than removing what is there.

options.label: Salt from the sea reacts with the calcium in the bone
options.feedback: The process happens in fresh groundwater as readily as anywhere near the sea; salt is not what is doing the work.

options.label: Mineral-rich water seeps into the bone and fills its tiny pores with stone
options.feedback: Groundwater carrying dissolved minerals moves slowly through the bone's spaces, and as those minerals crystallize inside, they harden the bone from within.

items.ok_line: Water carried the stone in, drop by drop, until the bone was rock.
items.ko_line: The bone was not destroyed and rebuilt; it was filled in from the inside.
items.exp_title: Filled in from the inside, drop by drop
items.exp_text: A buried bone is full of tiny spaces, both the larger marrow cavities and the fine pores throughout its structure. Groundwater trickling through the sediment carries minerals dissolved from the surrounding rock, and as that water passes through the bone over a long stretch of time, the minerals settle out of it and crystallize inside those spaces. The bone's own structure holds its shape throughout, so what eventually turns to stone keeps the fine details of the original down to its internal architecture.

items.prompt: How can a dinosaur's footprint survive as a fossil long after the mud it was pressed into has vanished?

options.label: The footprint turns directly into a puddle of tar
options.feedback: Tar preserves whole bodies trapped within it in a few famous places, but that is a separate process from a footprint pressed into mud.

options.label: A new layer of sediment covers the print before it erodes away
options.feedback: Sand, ash, or fine mud settling over the print sealed its shape in place before rain or wind could smooth it flat again.

options.label: The animal's foot leaves behind a chemical residue
options.feedback: A footprint's shape comes from the mud being physically pushed down, not from any substance left behind by the foot.

options.label: The mud instantly hardens into rock on contact
options.feedback: Mud does not turn to rock the moment a foot presses into it; hardening happens gradually, and only if the print survives long enough for that to occur.

items.ok_line: Covered just in time, so the shape below never got the chance to wash away.
items.ko_line: A print in wet mud does not last on its own; something has to protect it before the weather does.
items.exp_title: A shape protected just in time
items.exp_text: A foot pressed into soft mud leaves a dent in the exact shape of the sole that made it, but wet mud left exposed is soon smoothed away by rain or dries and crumbles in the wind. If a new layer of sediment settles over that print before either of those happens, the dent is sealed beneath it and protected from the weather that would otherwise have erased it. Buried that way, the print can hold its shape while the layers above and around it slowly harden into rock, long after the animal that made it is gone.

items.prompt: How does a piece of amber preserve an insect in such fine detail, down to delicate wings and hairs?

options.label: The insect is frozen inside a block of ice
options.feedback: Ice preserves mammoths and other cold-climate animals; amber is not ice, and it forms in places with no freezing involved.

options.label: The insect's body slowly dissolves and is replaced by amber
options.feedback: The insect is not dissolved and replaced; the resin instead surrounds and seals the body largely as it was.

options.label: Tree resin flows around the insect and hardens, sealing it away from air
options.feedback: Sticky resin oozing from a tree trapped the insect on contact, and as the resin hardened it sealed the insect off from the air and the organisms that cause decay.

options.label: Volcanic ash buries the insect and preserves its shell
options.feedback: Ash preserves shape by burial in sediment; amber comes from a sticky plant resin, a different substance and a different process entirely.

items.ok_line: Sealed in resin before decay ever had the chance to start.
items.ko_line: Amber begins as something sticky, oozing from a tree.
items.exp_title: Sealed away from the air, whole
items.exp_text: A tree wounded in some way oozes a sticky resin, and an insect that wanders into it or becomes coated by a fresh flow can be trapped before it can struggle free. As the resin hardens, it forms a seal around the insect that shuts out the air and the microorganisms that would otherwise break its body down. Cut off from decay this completely, structures as delicate as a wing's veins or the fine hairs on a leg can survive inside the hardened resin long after the tree itself has disappeared.

items.prompt: What is the difference between a fossil mold and a fossil cast?

options.label: A mold is the hollow shape left after the original dissolves away, and a cast is what forms when minerals later fill that hollow
options.feedback: Groundwater can dissolve the original bone or shell entirely, leaving an empty, exactly-shaped cavity; if minerals later seep in and harden inside that cavity, the result is a cast shaped just like the vanished original.

options.label: A mold forms on land and a cast forms underwater
options.feedback: Both can form in the same buried setting; what separates them is not where they form but whether the hollow has since been filled.

options.label: A mold is a fossil of a footprint and a cast is a fossil of a bone
options.feedback: Both terms describe the same two-step process, and either can happen to a footprint, a shell, or a bone alike.

options.label: A cast forms first, and a mold forms inside it later
options.feedback: The order runs the other way: the empty mold has to exist first, before anything can fill it and become a cast.

items.ok_line: An empty space first, then something poured into it.
items.ko_line: One of these is a hollow; the other is what later fills that hollow.
items.exp_title: An empty space, then something to fill it
items.exp_text: Buried bone or shell sometimes dissolves away entirely in acidic groundwater, leaving behind an empty cavity in the surrounding rock that carries every detail of the vanished surface — this hollow is the mold. If minerals dissolved in later groundwater seep into that same cavity and crystallize there, they take on the mold's exact shape as they harden, forming a cast that looks like the original even though none of the original material remains inside it.

items.prompt: Why can a mammoth frozen in permafrost preserve soft tissue like skin and hair, when most fossils preserve only bone?

options.label: Ice replaces the soft tissue with a mineral copy of it
options.feedback: Nothing is replaced in a frozen carcass; the original tissue itself is what survives, held in place by the cold rather than swapped for stone.

options.label: The cold prevents the bacteria that cause decay from working
options.feedback: Bacteria that break down soft tissue slow down sharply in the cold and stop working almost entirely once everything around them is frozen solid.

options.label: The mammoth's fur is naturally resistant to rot
options.feedback: Fur decays like any other soft tissue once conditions allow bacteria to work on it; what changes here is the surrounding temperature, not the fur itself.

options.label: Freezing turns the skin instantly into bone
options.feedback: Skin does not become bone under any circumstance; freezing preserves the skin as skin, unchanged in kind.

items.ok_line: Cold enough that decay simply could not get started.
items.ko_line: Think about what decay actually needs in order to happen at all.
items.exp_title: Cold enough to stop decay in its tracks
items.exp_text: Soft tissue normally breaks down because bacteria and other decay organisms feed on it, and that process runs faster in warmth and slows as the temperature drops. A body frozen quickly and kept frozen ever since sits at a temperature where those organisms can barely act, so the decay that would otherwise consume skin, muscle, and hair simply never gets underway. Tissue preserved this way can still show skin creased the way it was in life, and hair lying in the direction it grew, long after the animal itself died.

items.prompt: What can a fossilized dropping, or coprolite, reveal that fossil teeth alone cannot?

options.label: The exact sound the animal made
options.feedback: No fossil, dropping or otherwise, preserves sound; that leaves no physical trace at all.

options.label: The colour of the animal's skin
options.feedback: Skin colour is not carried in digested food remains; it would have to come from a preserved skin surface, not from a dropping.

options.label: The animal's exact age when it died
options.feedback: Age at death is read from clues like bone growth rings, not from the contents of a single dropping.

options.label: The fragments of what the animal actually ate, preserved directly
options.feedback: Bits of bone, plant fibre, or shell passed through the animal and hardened inside the dropping, giving direct physical evidence of a meal rather than a guess based on tooth shape.

items.ok_line: A last meal, preserved rather than guessed at.
items.ko_line: Think about what actually passes through an animal and ends up inside its droppings.
items.exp_title: A meal preserved rather than inferred
items.exp_text: Tooth shape can only suggest what an animal was equipped to eat, in the same way a knife's shape suggests what it might cut. A coprolite instead contains the leftover fragments of an actual meal — splinters of bone, chewed plant fibre, or crushed shell — that passed through the animal and hardened along with the rest of the dropping. Fragments identified this way tie a specific animal to a specific food it is known to have swallowed, rather than to food it was merely capable of eating.

items.prompt: Why are fossils found almost only in sedimentary rock, rather than in rock formed from cooled lava?

options.label: Sedimentary rock is the only kind that is ever old enough
options.feedback: Rock formed from lava can be just as old; age is not what separates the two here.

options.label: Lava rock is too dark for a fossil to be seen inside it
options.feedback: Colour has nothing to do with whether a fossil can form or survive; it is only about whether one can be seen at all.

options.label: A body is buried gently in settling sediment, while lava's heat would destroy it
options.feedback: Layers of mud, sand, or ash settle around a body without harming it, whereas molten rock is hot enough to burn away everything it touches before any shape could be preserved.

options.label: Sedimentary rock is softer, so fossils can be carved out of it
options.feedback: How easily a fossil is later removed has nothing to do with whether it could survive being formed in the first place.

items.ok_line: Buried gently by sediment, destroyed instantly by heat.
items.ko_line: Ask what actually happens to a body caught in each kind of rock as it forms.
items.exp_text: Sediment such as mud, sand, or volcanic ash settles around a body slowly and without heat, wrapping it in layers that can harden into rock over time while leaving its shape intact. Lava, by contrast, is hot enough to consume flesh and even bone on contact, so anything caught in it is destroyed rather than preserved. Only remains buried in the gentler process of settling sediment stand a chance of being carried, layer by layer, into the rock record.

items.prompt: How can a rock preserve the texture of skin or feathers when the skin and feathers themselves have completely rotted away?

options.label: Very fine sediment presses against the surface and holds its pattern even after the original decays
options.feedback: Fine-grained mud or ash settling directly against skin or feathers takes on their surface pattern in detail, and that pattern stays pressed into the sediment even once the soft material itself has rotted away.

options.label: The texture is painted onto the rock by minerals
options.feedback: No mineral process paints a picture; the texture comes from a physical impression left in the sediment itself.

options.label: The animal's skin turns to stone before it can decay
options.feedback: The original skin is not what survives; it decays as usual, and only the impression it left behind in the surrounding sediment remains.

options.label: Feathers are naturally resistant to decay, unlike skin
options.feedback: Feathers decay much like any other soft tissue; what preserves their shape here is the impression left in fine sediment, not any special resistance of their own.

items.ok_line: An impression left behind, long after the surface itself is gone.
items.ko_line: The original material rotted away completely; what is left is a pattern pressed into something else.
items.exp_title: A pattern outlives the surface that made it
items.exp_text: Very fine sediment, such as volcanic ash or soft mud, can settle directly against a body closely enough to take on the texture of its surface, down to the ridges of skin or the fine branches of a feather. That sediment then hardens around the body while decay works on the soft tissue itself, dissolving the original material away entirely. What is left behind in the hardened rock is not the skin or feather at all, but the shape it pressed into the sediment before it disappeared.

items.prompt: What can finding the fossils of several dinosaurs of different ages together in one place reveal, that a single skeleton alone cannot?

options.label: The exact colour patterns the animals displayed
options.feedback: Colour is occasionally read from preserved pigment structures, but that comes from fine tissue detail, not from how many skeletons are grouped together.

options.label: That the species lived and may have travelled or nested in groups
options.feedback: Adults and young found buried together points to animals that stayed near each other in life, rather than living and dying alone.

options.label: The precise sound the animals used to communicate
options.feedback: No fossil preserves sound in any form, whether found alone or grouped with others.

options.label: That the animals could all fly
options.feedback: Flight ability is judged from the shape of the limbs and body of an individual skeleton, not from how many skeletons are found nearby.

items.ok_line: A crowd of skeletons tells you something a single one never could.
items.ko_line: Think about what it means that these animals ended up buried in the same place at the same time.
items.exp_title: A crowd where a lone skeleton would leave a question
items.exp_text: A single skeleton can show what an animal looked like and how its body worked, but it says nothing about how that animal spent its life around others of its kind. Finding bones of adults and young of the same species buried together in one spot instead points to animals that moved, fed, or nested near each other rather than living apart. A nest full of eggs surrounded by adult bones close by tells a story an isolated skeleton never could, one of a group staying together rather than a solitary animal passing through.
